text.p: Gold remained under pressure on Friday with a fix in London at $371.30 per ounce, its lowest since April 25, 1994.
Copper dipped in volatile trading following a rise in LME stocks but prices ended off their lows.
Wheat eased in light trading but crude oil was firmer.
New York commodity markets were closed.
GOLD
Precious metals prices continued their downward slide on Friday and although they found a floor, dealers were dubious about it holding again next week.
Gold was fixed at $371.30 per ounce recording a fresh recent floor for bullion, which is at its lowest since April 25, 1994.

Selling into the Hong Kong and Tokyo markets by Australian producers, investment funds and out of Europe was cited as moving the gold price lower in the Far East. "Selling has been steady and the bearish sentiment overwhelming," one dealer said.
"We are so close to a round number ($370.00) that this is inevitably going to be suggested as a target," he added.
Market sources said the upsurge in spot selling by miners anxious to lock in prices to counter a falling market was a major physical factor behind falling prices.
"Producers have obviously been selling because if they are under hedged, there are going to be (price) levels at which they panic," one dealer said.
METALS
Copper fell in volatile trading following a rise in LME stocks by 2,425 tonnes but prices ended off their lows. Three months copper finished the day at $2,242, off $13 from Thursday's curb close.
A moderate rise in LME stocks, the first since early September, pushed prices lower on profit-taking and general liquidation.

But losses were kept to a minimum as the market was nervous about the upcoming December options declaration. The main concern was if December copper got close to $2,600 where there was a large concentration of open interest on calls.

"The stocks kept copper on the back foot for most of the day. But we've not seen a lot of weakness simply because of the options declarations on Wednesday," said analyst Robin Bhar of brokers Brandeis.
Aluminium traded in a tight range after slipping lower in early trading despite a decline in LME stocks by 4,925 tonnes.
It finished near its lows at $1,529.50 per tonne versus $1,555 on Thursday.
"It could have fallen further but forward interst helped underpin it," a dealer said.

Lead's fell to a 10-month low after a surprise rise in stocks. The lead inventory rose by 5,475 tonnes to 121,850 tonnes, the first time stocks have topped 120,000 tonnes since January. Lead's sentiment was undermined by a weakening technical background and the late start to winter demand for lead containing batteries. Lead ended the kerb at $686, down $8.
Zinc finished $3 firmer at $1,069 after a stocks fall of 4,925 tonnes while nickel dropped $100 to $6,820 per tonne following a stocks rise of 630 tonnes.

GRAINS - Wheat prices fell in light trading while New York commodity markets were closed Friday in an extended holiday. "Fund selling pressured wheat," said Ron Kucha, a Chicago grain trader with O'Connor & Co. "No deliveries on the December was a little supportive." Also bearish was news Turkey will seek up to 200,000 metric tons of wheat beginning December 10. Traders and analysts expected it to seek 500,000 metric tons. CBOT March wheat was down 6-3/4 cents at $3.77-1/2 per bushel.
OIL - Brent crude for January delivery closed 17 cents up at $22.82 per barrel with little fresh news to offer direction. NYMEX was closed for the extended Thanksgiving Day holiday.
